steps.title: Measure a safe drawing size
steps.goal: Convert CSS dimensions and display density to finite, bounded GPU pixel dimensions.
steps.trace: CSS width and height × display density → proportional GPU-limit cap → Viewport
steps.story:
Viewport converts CSS size and display density to GPU pixel dimensions. Reduce both dimensions together when they exceed the device limit. Reject hidden or invalid sizes.

Viewport is Copy, so drawing and camera setup can receive the same measured value. aspect uses the bounded pixel dimensions.

![CSS dimensions and density produce a bounded pixel viewport.](../illustrations/journey-direct-19a-viewport.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Density two doubles pixel dimensions without stretching the view; the GPU cap preserves proportions; hidden sizes are rejected.
steps.question: Why cap width and height by the same scale?
steps.answer: Independent caps would change their ratio and stretch the scene. A shared scale keeps proportions apart from integer rounding.
steps.experiment: Change the dense-display test ratio to 4.0 and lower the device limit to 1024. Predict the bounded dimensions before running the check.
steps.production: A camera aspect and its GPU attachments must use one bounded pixel size. This step establishes that size calculation; the next connects it to the browser and GPU.
steps.browser_status: Every document action follows the same editor path.
steps.browser_caption: Native tests establish bounded density-aware sizing. Chrome independently retains the editor input route and drawing; actual canvas and attachment resizing are connected next.

edits.why: Convert layout dimensions to a safe drawing size, keeping the proportions when the GPU limit applies.
Make the size calculation usable by browser code and Rust tests.

steps.title: Resize canvas, depth and camera together
steps.goal: Resize the drawing buffer, depth attachment and camera together, including on dense displays.
steps.trace: Resize event → Viewport → canvas pixels, surface, depth and aspect → command layout → draw
steps.question: Why resize the depth attachment with the canvas?
steps.answer: The colour and depth attachments in one render pass must have matching dimensions.
steps.story:
Use Viewport to resize canvas pixels, the surface, depth attachment and camera aspect together. Read the current CSS rectangle and display density before drawing.

The callback borrows the renderer and editor mutably. A hidden canvas returns without drawing; a changed size recreates attachments before the next frame.

![One viewport updates canvas, surface, depth and camera before drawing.](../illustrations/journey-direct-20-resize.svg)
steps.result: Resize the browser window. Geometry keeps its proportions and continues drawing across wide and tall sizes.
steps.experiment: Change the window from wide to tall, then type View Reset. The view should retain the current aspect.
steps.production: The final viewer uses the same size agreement for every attachment, including multisampling, picking and post-processing. Later panels need element resize observation as well as window events; this lesson handles window resizing and rechecks layout on each action.
steps.browser_status: Canvas pixels, depth and camera resize together.
steps.image_result: This frame is 770 × 385 pixels, a 2:1 viewport. Compare its wide shape with lesson 18’s 640 × 480 frame. The helper resizes the renderer through three sizes and checks the final face positions and shading. The final image alone cannot show the resize sequence; a browser resize recording is still needed.

steps.title: Remember the pointer that starts a drag
steps.goal: Retain one pointer and produce movement relative to its previous position.
steps.story:
Gesture remembers one pointer ID, its button and its positions. Reject a second press while that pointer is active. Each move reports the change from the previous position.

Option holds one Drag or none. as_mut borrows the stored drag; filter accepts only its pointer ID. The click threshold remembers whether any movement exceeded four CSS pixels.

![One press owns the drag; matching movement updates its remembered position.](../illustrations/journey-direct-20a-press.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Another pointer cannot replace the press or move it; matching moves report relative deltas.
steps.question: Why retain both the starting and previous positions?
steps.answer: The start distinguishes a click from a drag. The previous position gives the next orbit delta.
steps.experiment: Trace a matching pointer moving from [20.0, 25.0] to [30.0, 28.0] through the supplied press fixture. Predict the delta before reading its expected result.
steps.production: The browser will later deliver captured pointer events. This step establishes application ownership independently of DOM capture.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks establish one-pointer ownership and relative movement. Chrome retains the previous resize and command route; browser gestures are connected after release and action conversion.

edits.why: Retain one pointer, track its starting position and return relative right-drag movement.
Optional authoring fixture. Check rejected presses, pointer ownership and movement from the previous position.
Expose the gesture module to the browser and compile its tests only in the test build.

steps.browser_status: Canvas pixels, depth and camera resize together.
steps.title: Finish or cancel a drag
steps.goal: Release an owned pointer or cancel it without inventing a click.
steps.trace: Release → final move → take stored Drag → click or orbit; cancel → no active drag
steps.story:
Release processes the final position, then takes the remembered drag out of Gesture. A left release picks only if the press never crossed the movement threshold. Right release may supply one final orbit delta.

Cancellation clears the state without selecting. cancel_pointer checks ownership first; another pointer cannot end the active drag.

![Release finishes the remembered drag; cancellation clears it without a pick.](../illustrations/journey-direct-20b-release.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. A left drag returning to its start does not click; cancellation produces no selection and permits a fresh press.
steps.question: What does Option::take do on release?
steps.answer: It returns the stored Drag and leaves None, so later movement cannot continue the finished gesture.
steps.experiment: Read the return-to-start test. Predict the result if release checked only its final distance instead of the remembered moved flag.
steps.production: Lost capture, browser blur and interrupted tools must clear application gesture ownership. Their browser adapters follow after Motion reaches Editor.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks establish click classification, owned release and cancellation. Chrome still retains the earlier drawing and input route.

edits.why: Finish the owned pointer, preserve drag classification and clear cancelled input.
Optional authoring fixture. Check left-click classification, final motion, pointer ownership and cancellation.

steps.title: Convert pointer motion to editor actions
steps.goal: Convert CSS pointer coordinates and movement into existing Pick and Orbit actions.
steps.trace: Motion + CSS rectangle → Action → Editor → selection or view change
steps.story:
Motion::action uses the canvas CSS rectangle to convert a pick to normalized screen coordinates or a drag delta to orbit angles. Reject an invalid rectangle before dividing.

The method consumes Motion. Option<Action> permits invalid input to produce no editor request. Orbit changes the view while leaving document history unchanged.

![CSS pointer motion becomes a Pick or Orbit action through the existing editor.](../illustrations/journey-direct-20c-motion.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. A CSS centre maps to [0, 0]; orbit changes the camera, and Undo restores the document without rewinding it.
steps.question: Why use CSS dimensions instead of the GPU drawing size?
steps.answer: Pointer positions use CSS pixels. Mixing them with denser GPU pixels would change picking and sensitivity when display density changes.
steps.experiment: Double the rectangle dimensions and the pointer offsets in the centre test. Predict the same [0, 0] pick before running it.
steps.production: Pointer and command input share Editor actions. Camera navigation stays outside document history and browser callbacks do not edit geometry directly.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks route pointer motion through Editor and render its orbited view. Chrome independently retains the earlier input route until browser pointer delivery is connected next.

steps.title: Connect captured pointers to the editor
steps.goal: Orbit with a right drag, pick with a left click, and stop safely when the pointer or window loses focus.
steps.trace: DOM pointer → Gesture → Motion::action → Editor → redraw
steps.question: Why do we need both browser pointer capture and our own active pointer ID?
steps.answer: Capture keeps delivering events outside the canvas. The ID tells our application which pointer owns the gesture. Neither replaces the other: a second pointer must not finish the first gesture, and lost capture must clear our state.
steps.story:
Deliver canvas pointer events to Gesture when the command dock has not consumed them. Capture the accepted pointer so events keep arriving outside the canvas. Apply any returned action through Editor.

Release capture on pointer-up. Clear gesture state on cancellation, lost capture, blur or resize; suppress the browser context menu for right-drag navigation.

![Browser pointer capture and application gesture ownership meet at Editor actions.](../illustrations/journey-direct-21-gestures.svg)
steps.result: Right-drag the scene, then release. Further movement must stop orbiting; a left click still selects a face.
steps.experiment: Change the four-pixel click threshold to twenty. Try a short left drag, then restore four. Explain why this distance is measured in CSS pixels: doubling display density should not make the same hand movement harder to classify. Finally undo adding the box after orbiting. The box should disappear while the camera stays where you put it.
steps.production: The maintained viewer keeps richer gesture state and cancellation listeners in `src/app/input.rs`. This checkpoint establishes one active pointer and cancellation; touch orbit, wheel zoom and drawing tools will extend the same route rather than editing geometry inside DOM callbacks.

steps.title: Convert wheel units to camera zoom
steps.goal: Normalize pixels, lines and pages to bounded camera zoom without adding document history.
steps.trace: Wheel delta and units → CSS pixels → bounded exponential → Action::Zoom
steps.story:
navigation::wheel converts pixels, lines or pages to CSS pixels, caps one event at 600 pixels, then returns a positive exponential zoom factor. Invalid input returns None.

The stateless function borrows no editor. Its checks apply the returned Zoom through Editor and verify that camera movement stays outside document history.

![Wheel units become bounded CSS movement and a camera zoom action.](../illustrations/journey-direct-21a-wheel.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Equivalent pixel, line and page deltas give the same zoom; Undo restores geometry while retaining the camera.
steps.question: Why use an exponential for the zoom factor?
steps.answer: It stays positive and lets equal opposite movements restore the earlier distance, subject to the camera limits.
steps.experiment: Compare 48 pixels, three lines and 0.1 pages at height 480. Predict the same result before running the unit check.
steps.production: Mouse and phone navigation produce view actions outside document history. This step establishes wheel normalization before browser delivery.
steps.browser_status: Right-drag to orbit. Left-click to select. A cancelled drag stops immediately.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks normalize wheel units and render the resulting view. Chrome retains the previous pointer route; actual wheel delivery is connected next.

steps.title: Deliver wheel input without keyboard feature shortcuts
steps.goal: Normalize wheel input and keep every keyboard feature command in the command dock.
steps.trace: Wheel → navigation_action → Editor; printable key → command dock → typed Action
steps.question: Why request a non-passive wheel listener?
steps.answer: Handled wheel navigation must call prevent_default so the browser does not scroll the page.
steps.story:
Route wheel events through navigation::wheel, prevent page scrolling when zoom is handled, and keep printable keyboard input in the command dock. Focus the canvas when a pointer press starts navigation.

There is no keyboard feature map. Text-editing keys stay with the dock; Escape can cancel gesture state through the navigation route when the dock has not consumed it.

![Mouse navigation and typed command input share editor actions with distinct input ownership.](../illustrations/journey-direct-22-shortcuts.svg)
steps.result: Wheel over the scene to zoom. Click the canvas and type Pan Right; the first character reaches the dock and Enter pans the view.
steps.experiment: Change wheel sensitivity from 0.002 to 0.001, predict the difference, and try it before restoring the value. Run `Undo` after several wheel movements: it removes the box while preserving the camera. Run `Redo` to restore it. Explain why navigation does not enter document history. Finally Tab away during a drag; the canvas blur listener should cancel it.
steps.production: The maintained viewer routes mouse and phone navigation through src/app/input.rs. Printable input activates the command dock immediately; named commands share the existing state and history. This checkpoint keeps wheel zoom centred on the camera target. Pointer-centred zoom and phone gestures will extend navigation without introducing keyboard feature shortcuts.
